title: Algorithmic Fairness
explain_beginner: Many people worry that computer programs used to make decisions, like who gets a loan or a college spot, might treat people unfairly because of their race. A common idea is to hide race from the program. This paper says that idea is wrong and can even cause harm. The authors explain that fairness should not change how the program makes its predictions. Instead, fairness can change how those predictions are used, such as using different cutoffs for different groups. In an example about college admissions, they found that including race as a factor can actually make decisions both fairer and more effective.
explain_business: This research shows that trying to make algorithms fair by removing race can backfire. Instead, companies should keep race in their models if it improves predictions, but then apply fairness by adjusting how those predictions are used, such as different thresholds for different groups. In practice, this means lenders and other decision-makers must document the trade-off between model accuracy and explainability. The decision this informs is whether to blind algorithms to race, which the paper argues against, and instead to focus on how predictions are turned into decisions, while being transparent about the costs.
explain_practitioner: The paper challenges the common practice of blinding algorithms to race. The authors argue that fairness preferences should not alter the choice of estimator. Instead, they should only affect how the estimated prediction function is applied, for example by using group-specific thresholds. The prediction function itself should remain unchanged. They demonstrate this with an empirical example on college admissions, showing that including race as a variable can improve both equity and efficiency. The editor's note adds that the work applies fairness metrics to real mortgage data and highlights an explainability cost of better models, a trade-off lenders must document.
